title: A slow read of Neural Networks Are Already Clean
text:
These are working notes on Nick Cammarata’s essay Neural Networks Are Already Clean (Goodfire, 2026). The audience is people with a physics background who are curious about interpretability but have not worked in it. The aim is to go through the essay slowly, one section at a time, filling in the background each section assumes and re-creating its claims in the smallest instructive setting that fits on a single consumer GPU.
The essay itself is long (about 27,000 words with its appendix) and is written as a working hypothesis rather than a paper. Its central claim is that the famous examples of “polysemantic” neurons, the ones that seemed to respond to unrelated things and that motivated the superposition hypothesis, were misread. On the author’s account the mess came from broken tools, weak architectures, incomplete explanations, and a growth pattern he calls recursive generalization, all of which are fixable or benign. True superposition, unrelated things folded into one neuron, should be the last hypothesis rather than the first.

title: The Short Version
text: The opening section is the whole essay in miniature. This page lists what it claims, sorts the claims by how testable they are, and notes where in these notes each one is taken up. No experiments here; the section is a statement of position.

title: The Short Version
text:
The argument in one paragraph
The field found neurons that seemed to respond to unrelated things (polysemanticity), and explained them with superposition: a network short of neurons folds unrelated things together because they rarely co-occur. If true, the neurons are a knot with nothing to learn from, and the only route is to train a second model (a sparse autoencoder) that unfolds it. The essay says the canonical evidence for this was misread. The messy late layers of InceptionV1 were an architecture and tooling failure that modern architectures fixed by accident; the famous cat-and-car neuron and the car-into-dogs circuit were ordinary generalisation and composition; and the residual apparent polysemanticity is mostly recursive generalisation, a neuron sprouting related offshoots as it grows. That leaves one learning principle, generalisation, which happens to be fractal. So the network’s own neurons and circuits can be studied directly, and this works in practice up to trillion-parameter models.

title: The Short Version
text:
Two ways to do interpretability
The essay frames everything around a choice.

Normal science on the network itself. Look at neurons and circuits, watch data flow through them, run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. This is where the field started (the Distill Circuits thread, 2020).
Start from a hypothesised feature list and design reconstruction objectives to extract it, “usually ignoring the original”. This is the sparse-autoencoder programme the field moved to after 2022.

The essay’s position is that the field fell back from the first to the second on the strength of evidence that does not hold up, and that the first approach now works. Note the rhetorical asymmetry: option 2 is described as ignoring the original network. Practitioners of SAEs would say they study the original through a better basis. Worth raising in discussion.

Claims about method and history

Early explainer models could not run conjecture-and-test loops; metrics rewarded simulating activations rather than being right; people looked for the wrong motifs (nouns rather than feelings, social cues, punctuation summaries); most studies used small simplified models.
Understanding compounds like a crossword: once most of the map is filled in, each new neuron is constrained by its neighbours, and the unexplained remainder points at broken tools.
Bigger models learn narrower neurons, so size helps rather than hurts.
“Understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most.”

These are not falsifiable in a single experiment but they make predictions about how an auditing effort should scale, and we can at least check the narrowing-with-size claim on our own model sweep.


The four-step argument, and where its weight sits

One learning principle, not two. (The empirical heart. Everything in §03–§09 is evidence for this.)
Normal science on modern models goes better than expected. (Mostly testimony about agent-scale auditing; §10.)
Understanding compounds. (A claim about process; hard to test, easy to believe once 1 and 2 hold.)
Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need.

The essay is careful to label step 4 as speculation. Steps 1 and 2 carry the argument.

title: The Short Version
section: Things to notice on a first read
text:
Things to notice on a first read

The author co-authored both hypotheses. He found the original superposition circuit in 2019 and the “conjoined features” observation in 2021. The essay is a recantation of the first in favour of the second. This matters for how to weigh the testimony: the evidence that convinced him is mostly things he looked at, and the sample sizes he gives are explicitly small.
The headline percentages are soft. Footnote 1 says the 90% figure moves with the weak-activation threshold, depth, and what counts as one thing, and the author says he included a number only because reviewers wanted one. The claim that matters is the qualitative one: mixtures are related, not arbitrary.
“Nothing reads that combination.” This is the sharpest sentence in the section. The original superposition story required a downstream reader that unpacked the car from the dog neurons. The essay’s claim is that no such reader exists. That is checkable from the weights.
The bitter-lesson analogy is doing argumentative work: “scaling ordinary investigation beats engineering a clever new decomposition”. It is an analogy, not evidence.

title: The Short Version
text:
Questions for discussion

Superposition and recursive generalisation make opposite predictions about what shares a neuron. What would a decisive test look like in a model we can train ourselves, and what confounds would make the two hard to tell apart in a finished model with no checkpoints?
If a small model’s neurons are merely coarse (one “car” neuron for all cars), is that distinguishable in practice from superposition of many car types? What does “coarse” mean operationally?
The essay treats “the neuron basis is privileged” as settled by the elementwise nonlinearity. For SwiGLU neurons with a gate and a value, is the neuron still the right unit, or is the pair?
Does “nothing reads that combination” generalise into a usable criterion: a representation is only in superposition if some downstream weight reads the packed combination?

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
The essay assumes its reader already knows what a neuron is, what a feature is, why anyone would train a sparse autoencoder, and what an attribution graph shows. This page fills that in for someone with a physics background and no interpretability background. It is deliberately concrete: every object is defined by an equation or a procedure, and the vocabulary the essay uses is collected in a glossary at the end.
If you already work in interpretability, skip to the glossary and the map for physicists.

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
1. Neurons
A trained network is a fixed function f_\theta from inputs to outputs. “Interpretability” in the sense of this essay means explaining how it computes that function in terms of its internal parts, the way a biologist explains an organism in terms of cells and organs rather than in terms of its genome.
The basic internal part is the neuron. In a fully-connected (MLP) layer with input vector x \in \mathbb{R}^d, neuron i has an input weight vector w_i \in \mathbb{R}^d, a bias b_i, and a scalar nonlinearity \phi:

a_i(x) = \phi\big(w_i \cdot x + b_i\big).

The quantity w_i\cdot x + b_i is the preactivation; a_i is the activation. The layer’s output is then a linear map of the activation vector, y = \sum_i a_i\, v_i, where v_i is neuron i’s output weight vector. So each neuron reads one direction (w_i) and writes one direction (v_i), with a scalar nonlinearity in between. The essay’s language of “readers” and “what a neuron lets through” is literal: downstream neurons whose w_j has a large component along v_i are the readers of neuron i.
Three nonlinearities matter here:

ReLU, \phi(z) = \max(z, 0). Used in InceptionV1 and most pre-2020 vision models. The negative side of the preactivation is thrown away.
GELU, a smooth version of ReLU, \phi(z) = z\,\Phi(z) with \Phi the Gaussian CDF. Used in GPT-2 and ConvNeXt. Slightly negative for small negative z, which is why the essay can talk about a neuron’s negative side even in GELU networks.
SwiGLU (gated), used in Llama, Qwen, and most modern language models. The neuron has two input weight vectors, a gate g_i and a value u_i, and 
a_i(x) = \mathrm{SiLU}(g_i\cdot x)\,(u_i\cdot x), \qquad \mathrm{SiLU}(z) = \frac{z}{1+e^{-z}}.
 Since \mathrm{SiLU}(z) is slightly negative for z<0, the product is positive when both the gate and the value are negative. The essay calls this the “double-negative regime” and argues it is an architectural artefact, so keep it in mind.

The negative pole. Even with ReLU, the preactivation w_i\cdot x + b_i can be driven strongly negative by some inputs. The essay insists that this negative side is meaningful: the weights w_i are learned as a sum of “votes”, and whatever pushes the preactivation down is, by construction, the thing the neuron is built to not respond to. The essay’s canonical example is a neuron whose positive pole is “V-shaped” and whose negative pole is “round”. It uses the word pole for each side.
Neurons in convolutional networks. In a conv net the “neuron” is a channel: a filter w_i that is applied at every spatial position, giving an activation map a_i(x, \text{pos}) rather than a single number. InceptionV1 neuron “4e:55” means channel 55 of the layer named mixed4e. When the essay shows an image that “activates” a neuron it usually means the maximum, or sum, of the map over positions.
Neurons in transformers. A transformer block has an attention sublayer and an MLP sublayer. The “neurons” are the hidden units of the MLP: for a model with residual width d_{\text{model}} the MLP expands to d_{\text{mlp}} \approx 4\, d_{\text{model}} (or \approx \tfrac{8}{3} d_{\text{model}} for SwiGLU) hidden units, each of which is a neuron in exactly the sense above. There is one activation per neuron per token. Qwen3-32B has 64 layers with 25,600 neurons each, so about 1.6 million neurons, which is the “more than a million neurons” the essay mentions. Attention heads are not neurons and the essay treats them separately.

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
2. The residual stream
Modern networks (ResNets, ConvNeXt, every transformer) are residual: each layer adds its output to a running vector rather than replacing it,

x_{\ell+1} = x_\ell + f_\ell(x_\ell).

The running vector x_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}} is the residual stream. In a transformer there is one such vector per token position. Every neuron in every layer reads from the stream by taking an inner product with its w_i and writes back to it by adding a multiple of its v_i. The stream is therefore a shared, high-dimensional bus; the only nonlinear operations are the elementwise \phi inside the MLPs, the softmax inside attention, and the normalisation (LayerNorm: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation across the d_{\text{model}} components, then rescale) that precedes each sublayer.
Two facts about the stream drive much of the essay:

It has no privileged basis. Rotating the stream by an orthogonal matrix R, and correspondingly rotating every w_i \to R w_i and v_i \to R v_i, gives an identical network. Nothing about a single coordinate of the stream has any meaning. Neuron activations, by contrast, do have a privileged basis, because \phi acts elementwise: rotating the neurons changes the function. This is why “look at the neurons” is a well-posed instruction and “look at the stream’s coordinates” is not.
InceptionV1 has no residual stream (it predates ResNets). Each layer must carry everything the next layer needs. The essay argues that this, rather than any inherent property of learning, is why InceptionV1’s late layers looked like a mess, and it uses the absence of a residual stream to design a squeeze experiment later on.

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
3. Attention, briefly
An attention head at layer \ell moves information between token positions. For each pair of positions (s, t) it computes a score from the query at t and the key at s, softmaxes the scores over s to get weights A_{ts}, and then adds to the stream at t the weighted sum \sum_s A_{ts}\, W_O W_V\, x_s. The essay’s four questions about a head are: where it looks (A_{ts}, cheap to read off), what it looks for (the query-key circuit), what it does when it finds it (the output-value circuit, which can be read in terms of which neurons’ v_i it picks up and which neurons’ w_j it lands on), and why. The essay only claims progress on the first three and says little about the fourth.

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
4. Features and the two hypotheses
A feature is, informally, a property of the input that the network represents. The word is notoriously hard to make precise and the essay’s appendix has a note on exactly this problem. The working definition in most of the field is the linear representation hypothesis: a feature is a direction d_k in some activation space, and the degree to which the feature is present in input x is the projection of the activation onto d_k.
If the feature directions happened to coincide with neuron directions, every neuron would respond to exactly one human-recognisable thing. Such a neuron is called monosemantic. A neuron that seems to respond to several unrelated things is polysemantic. The famous example, and the essay’s opening target, is InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55, which the 2020 Zoom In paper reported as responding to both cat faces and car fronts.
Two explanations for polysemanticity were on the table before this essay:

Superposition. The network wants to represent more features than it has neurons, so it assigns features to nearly orthogonal directions that are not neuron-aligned. Each neuron then carries small pieces of several unrelated features. The next page reproduces the toy model that made this precise. Under this hypothesis the neurons are the wrong basis, and the right move is to decompose the activations into the underlying features by some optimisation (a sparse autoencoder).
Generalisation / composition. The neuron really does respond to one thing, but that thing is not a noun we have a word for (“V-shape” rather than “cat or car”), or the neuron grew outward from a core onto related territory during training (“recursive generalisation”). Under this hypothesis the neurons are the right basis and the task is to explain them better.

These make opposite predictions about what should be bundled together: superposition bundles things because they are unrelated (so that they rarely co-occur and interfere little), generalisation bundles things because they are related. The essay’s entire argument is that the evidence points to the second.

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
5. How people look at neurons
The tools below are the “microscope” the essay says was mis-set. Each is simple to state.
Top-activating examples. Run a large dataset through the network, record each neuron’s activation on every input (or every token), and sort. The top few dozen inputs are the cheapest description of a neuron, and automated labelling pipelines mostly look at these. The essay’s “weak activations” section is about everything below the top of this list.
Feature visualisation. Instead of searching a dataset, synthesise an input by gradient ascent on the activation, x^\star = \arg\max_x a_i(x), starting from noise. Done naively this produces adversarial high-frequency noise. The 2017 Feature Visualization paper made it work by parametrising the image in a decorrelated Fourier basis and by transformation robustness: optimise the expected activation under random jitter, scaling and rotation of the image, so the optimiser must find a pattern that excites the neuron the way a real image would. The essay’s point about “reward hacking” is that in late layers the optimiser still finds a route the network rarely uses on real data (it draws dogs when the real circuit carries car information), and that this is a property of the tool, not the neuron.
Ablation. Set a neuron’s activation to zero (or to its dataset mean) on a given input and measure what changes in the output. This is the interventional test behind statements like “remove the eight neurons with a Santa negative side and the Santa probability falls from near-certain to 6 percent”.
Attribution. For a given input, estimate how much neuron i in one layer contributes to neuron j in a later layer. The simplest version is the product of a_i and the gradient \partial a_j / \partial a_i, which is exact when the path between them is linear. In a residual network the path from v_i to w_j through the stream is exactly linear, so the direct effect is just a_i\,(v_i\cdot w_j), and the only approximation is in how the indirect effects through intervening nonlinearities are handled.
Attribution graphs. Take one prompt, compute attributions between all pairs of units across all layers, keep the strong edges, and draw the result as a graph from input tokens to output logits. Anthropic’s 2025 circuit tracing work builds these graphs on transcoder features rather than neurons. A transcoder is a trained replacement for each MLP with a sparse, wide hidden layer, chosen so that the hidden units are more interpretable than the original neurons. The cost is that the replacement model is only approximately the original: the essay quotes Anthropic’s own methods page for the figure that it predicts the same next token only about half the time. The essay’s language-model claim is that the same graphs can be built on the original neurons with no replacement model at all.
Steering. Add a multiple of v_i to the stream during generation and see what the model does. Used in the essay as an informal check (“steering the Colorado neuron makes the model want to go hiking”).

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
6. Sparse autoencoders (dictionary learning)
If superposition is true, activation vectors x \in \mathbb{R}^d are sparse non-negative combinations of n \gg d feature directions, x \approx \sum_k f_k(x)\, d_k with few f_k \neq 0. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) tries to recover the dictionary \{d_k\} and the coefficients f_k by training

f(x) = \mathrm{ReLU}(W_{\text{enc}}\, x + b_{\text{enc}}), \qquad
\hat x = W_{\text{dec}}\, f(x) + b_{\text{dec}},

to minimise \|x - \hat x\|^2 + \lambda \|f(x)\|_1 over a large dataset of activations. The \ell_1 penalty enforces sparsity; the columns of W_{\text{dec}} are the learned feature directions. A TopK SAE replaces the penalty by keeping only the k largest preactivations per input, which is what the essay uses (640 features, k=2). “Dictionary learning” is the general name for this family.
Two numbers are always reported. Variance explained says how well \hat x reconstructs x. More honest is to splice the SAE into the network, replacing x by \hat x at that layer, and measure how much the network’s accuracy or loss degrades, because small reconstruction error can still destroy information the network needed. The essay reports both for its squeeze experiment.
The essay is not against SAEs as such. Its claim is that, in the networks it studied, an SAE mostly rediscovers the neurons (88 percent of SAE activity on ConvNeXt’s last layer is a near copy of a single neuron) and the rest is loose regroupings of them, and that on InceptionV1 4e:55 the SAE “fractures” a single V-shape neuron into a car feature and a cat feature, which is further from what the neuron does.

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
8. A map for physicists
Some intuitions carry over cleanly; others actively mislead. A short list.

Superposition is a compressed-sensing statement. n sparse signals in d < n dimensions can be stored and recovered if their directions are nearly orthogonal (Johnson–Lindenstrauss: one can fit e^{O(\epsilon^2 d)} vectors in \mathbb{R}^d with pairwise overlaps below \epsilon). The toy model on the next page is a learned version of this with ReLU as the decoder. The essay accepts the mathematics and disputes whether real networks are in the regime where the trade-off (capacity vs interference) is the dominant consideration.
“Circuit racing” is mode competition. The essay’s account of why networks generalise is that broad features fire on more of the data, receive more gradient, and starve the narrow ones. This is rich-get-richer dynamics in the sense of a linear instability: whichever direction has the largest growth rate dominates. The companion idea in the literature is “gradient starvation” and “coherent gradients”.
The privileged basis is a symmetry statement. The residual stream has an O(d) symmetry; the neuron layer breaks it to permutations (and sign flips, in some cases) because \phi is elementwise. Asking which basis is “real” is asking which symmetry the dynamics breaks.
Recursive generalisation vs superposition is a locality question. Generalisation is local in some similarity metric on the data; superposition is non-local by design. This is the one empirical dichotomy the essay turns on, and watching a neuron over training checkpoints is the proposed experiment.
Beware “feature” as a conserved quantity. The essay’s appendix argues that the toy model prices the cost of sharing a neuron (interference) but not the benefit (reuse by downstream readers), because in the toy there is nothing downstream. In a real network a representation only matters through what reads it. A physicist’s instinct to count degrees of freedom and ask whether n > d is, on the essay’s account, the wrong question.
Beware the “microscope” analogy as reassurance. A real microscope’s artefacts are well understood; the essay’s whole historical section is about artefacts in feature visualisation and in the choice of model organism that went unrecognised for years.

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
Glossary
Terms in the essay’s own sense, in roughly the order they appear.

Polysemantic / monosemantic. A neuron that appears to respond to several unrelated things / to one thing. The essay argues the first is largely an observer’s statement.
Superposition. Unrelated features stored in overlapping, non-neuron-aligned directions because the network has run out of neurons. The essay distinguishes three senses: (a) more features than dimensions, which a clean network could also satisfy; (b) a learning principle that packs unrelated things into neurons, which is what the essay argues against; (c) the same principle applied to directions in the residual stream.
Recursive generalisation. A neuron starts on one core and sprouts related offshoots as training proceeds, “the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches”. Earlier called “conjoined features” in the multimodal-neurons paper.
Pole. The positive or negative side of a neuron’s preactivation. Both are treated as meaningful.
Gate. A neuron viewed as control flow: what it lets through and what it keeps out, rather than what noun it names.
Circuit. A set of neurons across layers connected by large weights, doing an identifiable sub-computation.
Motif. A pattern that recurs across many circuits (e.g. “summary on punctuation”, “say or just think”, pose neurons feeding class detectors).
Weak activations. Everything below the top of a neuron’s activation distribution; the essay argues they are mostly generalisation and mostly ablatable.
Blind maximum. Test an explanation by having a second agent, who sees only the explanation, write an input intended to maximally activate the neuron. If it beats the dataset maximum the explanation captured the centre of the neuron.
Neuron paper. A short written audit of one neuron, produced by an agent; the essay reports statistics over 1,000 of them.
Attribution graph. A per-prompt graph of which units drive which, from tokens to logits.
Enumerative vs exploratory interpretability. Build a complete list of features to audit, vs start from questions and move through the network as needed. The essay favours the second and says the first was “always a means to an end”.
Already clean. The essay’s thesis: the network’s own parts are built to be read by its own downstream parts, and are therefore readable by us without being decomposed first.

title: Preliminaries: the objects the essay talks about
text:
Questions from the reading group
Raised in discussion on 22 October 2026. The answers are ours, not the essay’s.
Under the recursive-generalisation picture, is the number of features capped at the number of neurons?
At the level of neuron-sized features, more or less yes. Each neuron, or each pole, is one coarse concept with a tree of related offshoots, so the number of first-class concepts in a layer is about twice the neuron count. The essay accepts this and treats it as fine, for three reasons.

Granularity scales with room. A small model has one car neuron; a large one has many kinds of car. The missing distinctions in the small model are not hidden anywhere; the model does not make them. The toy-model page shows this directly: twenty inputs are represented as four directions, and the within-group identity is simply absent until a reader wants it.
Composition is not superposition. “Dog in frontal pose” is represented by a dog neuron and a pose neuron firing together, each independently meaningful. Readers use conjunctions without any cancellation, so the number of distinguishable situations is combinatorial without any neuron being a mixture. The essay cites Anthropic’s note on exactly this distinction.
Depth adds levels. Offshoots in one layer become first-class neurons in the next.

The essay’s broader move is to say that counting features was never the goal: what matters is whether every distinction the network uses can be traced to neurons and circuits, and the question “are there more features than dimensions” is, in its words, mostly irrelevant. Whether to accept that reframing is a fair thing to argue about.
So is the cap per layer or per network? Is the maximum roughly the residual-stream width, or do different layers hold different features so that the counts add?
The counts add. The cap is per layer of MLP neurons, different layers hold different features, and the neuron-level total is the sum over layers. Qwen3-32B has 64 layers of 25,600 neurons, about 1.6 million, against a residual stream of width 5,120: neuron-level features outnumber stream dimensions by roughly 300 to 1. The same holds in a modern conv net.
The residual stream is therefore not a cap on the number of features. It is a cap on how many can be simultaneously present and linearly separable at one position, and even that has slack. Four things reconcile 1.6 million writers with 5,120 dimensions:

Features are not simultaneously active. At any token only a small fraction of neurons fire. The stream is a bus, not a storage array, so what has to fit at once is the active set, not the catalogue.
Directions are reused across depth. A direction written by layer 10 and read by layer 14 can be overwritten or ignored afterwards, and layer 40 can use it for something else.
Related neurons write nearby directions. Many car-part neurons write into a shared car region, which is composition rather than packing.
Near-orthogonality is cheap in high dimension. This is the Johnson–Lindenstrauss slack, and it is the one place where the strict sense of superposition genuinely lives in the stream.

That last point is where the essay is most careful and least decisive. It concedes that packing in the stream, its sense (c), may be impossible to rule out, and claims only that it has not been a bottleneck in practice: neuron reads and writes come out clean, and attribution graphs come out clean. Its supporting evidence is the “crushing” experiment, in which a 7-million-parameter conv net was retrained with its stream four and eight times narrower, down to 46 dimensions in the last block, keeping the neurons. Accuracy fell from 72% to 60% and then 39%, but the map of what the neurons do looked the same, only messier. The information flowing through the stream at any moment is far lower dimensional than the count of things that ever flow through it.
The honest summary: the number of concepts a network can represent is set by its neurons, summed over layers, and by compositions of them. The stream width constrains concurrency and separability, not the catalogue. Whether the concurrent set is ever packed non-locally in the stream is the residual claim the essay leaves open, and it is where a sceptic should push.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
text:
Before reading the essay’s “Superposition” section it helps to have run the toy model that made superposition a precise idea: Elhage et al., Toy Models of Superposition (Anthropic, 2022). The essay’s appendix calls it “careful work, the kind our field should aspire to” and says it found no problems with its experiments. Its objection is to the framing: the toy prices the cost of sharing a neuron (interference) but not the benefit (reuse by downstream readers), because in the toy nothing is downstream.
This page does three things. It reproduces the toy’s main results in a few seconds of CPU time, it reproduces the essay’s modification (correlated inputs plus a layer of hidden neurons), and it states what we should carry forward into the essay proper.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
text:
1. The setup
There are n features, collected in a vector x \in [0,1]^n. Feature i is present with probability 1-S, with amplitude uniform on [0,1], and absent (exactly zero) otherwise. S is the sparsity. The network must squeeze x through a bottleneck of width m < n and recover it:

h = W x \in \mathbb{R}^m, \qquad \hat x = \mathrm{ReLU}(W^{\mathsf T} h + b).

The loss is a weighted reconstruction error \sum_i I_i\,(x_i - \hat x_i)^2 with importances I_i = 0.9^i, so earlier features matter more. The whole model is the m \times n matrix W and the bias b. Column W_i \in \mathbb{R}^m is the direction in the bottleneck that feature i is written to and read from.
Why ReLU on the output matters: with a linear decoder the best the model can do is PCA, keeping the top m features and dropping the rest. ReLU lets it do better, because small interference from other features can be clipped off at zero if the interfering features are usually absent. That is the whole mechanism of superposition: sparsity makes interference cheap.
The diagnostics used below, all computable from W:

\|W_i\|: how strongly feature i is represented at all (0 means dropped).
The superposition index \sum_{j\ne i} (\hat W_i\cdot W_j)^2: how much other features overlap with feature i’s direction. Zero means a private direction.
The dimensionality D_i = \|W_i\|^2 / \sum_j (\hat W_i\cdot W_j)^2. A feature with its own orthogonal direction has D_i = 1; two features sharing a direction antipodally have D_i = \tfrac12; the paper shows the values cluster at simple fractions.



Imports and helpers
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd().parent))
import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from common.toy_models import (TMS, TMSHidden, train, sample_independent, sample_grouped,
                               feature_norms, superposition_index, feature_dimensionality,
                               cosine_matrix)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 9})

def fit_tms(n, m, S, steps=4000, seed=0, importance_decay=0.9):
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    model = TMS(n, m, gen)
    imp = torch.tensor([importance_decay**i for i in range(n)])
    sampler = lambda b, g: sample_independent(b, n, S, g)
    train(model, sampler, imp, steps=steps, seed=seed)
    return model

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
section: 2. From “keep the top m” to packing, as sparsity rises
text:
2. From “keep the top m” to packing, as sparsity rises
The paper’s headline figure: n=20 features in m=5 dimensions, trained at increasing sparsity. Each panel shows the Gram matrix W^{\mathsf T}W (which features overlap with which) and, below it, each feature’s norm coloured by its superposition index.


Train n=20, m=5 across sparsity
n, m = 20, 5
sparsities = [0.0, 0.7, 0.9, 0.97, 0.99]
models = {S: fit_tms(n, m, S, steps=8000) for S in sparsities}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, len(sparsities), figsize=(2.2*len(sparsities), 4.6),
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1.6]})
for j, S in enumerate(sparsities):
    W = models[S].W.detach()
    G = (W.T @ W).numpy()
    ax = axes[0, j]
    ax.imshow(G, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    ax.set_title(f"S = {S}   (1/(1-S) = {1/(1-S):.0f})", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax = axes[1, j]
    norms = feature_norms(W); sup = superposition_index(W)
    ax.bar(range(n), norms, color=plt.cm.viridis(np.clip(sup, 0, 1)))
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1.15); ax.set_xticks([]);
    if j == 0: ax.set_ylabel("‖W_i‖")
plt.tight_layout()





Top row: W^{\mathsf T}W. Bottom row: \|W_i\| per feature, coloured by superposition index (dark = private direction, yellow = heavily shared). At S=0 the model keeps the five most important features and drops the rest. As features become rarer it represents more of them, first in antipodal pairs, then in denser arrangements.




Reading the figure. With dense features (S=0) every feature is on almost every time, so any overlap is paid for on every sample; the model keeps the five most important features on orthogonal axes and drops the other fifteen. As features become rare, the expected cost of interference falls like (1-S) while the benefit of representing an extra feature does not, so more and more features are packed in. The first packing is antipodal pairs (two features on the same axis with opposite sign: the ReLU separates them because they are rarely both present), then denser polytopes.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
text:
3. The geometry of packing
With m = 2 we can draw the columns W_i directly.


Train n=5 and n=6 features into m=2 dims at high sparsity
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(9, 4.6))
for r, nn_ in enumerate([5, 6]):
    for j, S in enumerate([0.0, 0.8, 0.95, 0.995]):
        W = fit_tms(nn_, 2, S, steps=3000, importance_decay=1.0, seed=1).W.detach().numpy()
        ax = axes[r, j]
        for i in range(nn_):
            ax.annotate("", xy=W[:, i], xytext=(0, 0),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=plt.cm.tab10(i), lw=1.6))
            ax.text(*(1.12*W[:, i]), str(i), color=plt.cm.tab10(i), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
        ax.set_xlim(-1.3, 1.3); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.3); ax.set_aspect("equal")
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
        ax.set_title(f"n={nn_}, S={S}", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()





Feature directions W_i in a two-dimensional bottleneck. At low sparsity only two features survive. At high sparsity the model spreads all of them around a regular polygon (pentagon, hexagon), the arrangement that minimises the worst-case overlap.




A pentagon in two dimensions is the simplest picture of superposition: five directions, none orthogonal to any other, each with overlap \cos 72^\circ \approx 0.31 with its two neighbours. Any single feature is read with a little contamination from its neighbours, but if at most one is present at a time the ReLU on the output removes the contamination exactly. The price is that when two neighbours are present together, both reconstructions are wrong.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
text:
4. Dimensionality per feature is quantised
Scaling up the counts shows the paper’s most striking observation: the amount of bottleneck each feature gets, D_i, does not vary continuously with sparsity but jumps between a few discrete values that correspond to regular geometric arrangements.


Train n=80, m=20 across many sparsity values and scatter D_i
n, m = 80, 20
S_list = [0.0, 0.5, 0.75, 0.875, 0.94, 0.97, 0.985, 0.992, 0.996]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
for S in S_list:
    W = fit_tms(n, m, S, steps=4000, importance_decay=0.97, seed=2).W
    D = feature_dimensionality(W)
    x = 1/(1-S) * (1 + 0.04*np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(n))
    ax.scatter(x, D, s=8, alpha=0.6, color="C0")
for y, lab in [(1, "1"), (0.5, "1/2"), (0.4, "2/5"), (1/3, "1/3")]:
    ax.axhline(y, color="gray", lw=0.6, ls="--"); ax.text(1.05, y+0.015, lab, fontsize=8, color="gray")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("1 / (1 − S)"); ax.set_ylabel("dimensionality $D_i$")
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.1)
plt.tight_layout()





Dimensionality per feature against 1/(1-S) (log scale). Each point is one feature. Values pile up at 1 (own axis), 1/2 (antipodal pair), and fractions like 2/5 and 1/3 that correspond to pentagons and triangles in sub-spaces of the bottleneck. Dropped features sit at 0.




At low sparsity the features split cleanly between “own axis” (D_i = 1), “antipodal pair” (D_i = \tfrac12) and “dropped” (D_i = 0). As sparsity rises the represented features move to lower plateaus and eventually, when every feature is represented, settle near m/n = 0.25, the uniform share. The paper’s figure, with n = 400 features and m = 30 dimensions and much longer training, resolves more of the intermediate plateaus (2/5 for pentagons, 1/3 for triangles and so on) than this quick run does. The plateaus are what the paper means by phase changes: as sparsity increases, the optimal arrangement jumps discretely from one polytope to another. A physicist will recognise this as a continuous control parameter selecting among discrete symmetric configurations. It is a genuine and robust result and the essay does not dispute it.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
section: 5. The essay’s modification: correlated inputs plus hidden neurons
text:
5. The essay’s modification: correlated inputs plus hidden neurons
Now the part the essay added. Its appendix says: “When we put correlated inputs and hidden neurons in one model, related inputs grew onto the neurons. Making inputs fire more often pushed the toy toward what the paper calls ‘PCA-like’ solutions, combining related inputs into shared representations.”
Two changes to the toy.

Correlated data. Instead of independent features, 20 inputs are arranged in 4 groups of

A whole group turns on together with probability p; within an active group each member gets an independent amplitude. This is the toy version of “in real data almost nothing is related to nothing”.

A hidden layer. After the 5-dimensional bottleneck there is a layer of k ReLU neurons before the output: a = \mathrm{ReLU}(V h + c), \hat x = U a + b. These are the “neurons” whose cleanliness we can now ask about; the original toy has none.



Train the grouped model, sparse and dense
n_groups, group_size, m, k = 4, 5, 5, 10
n = n_groups * group_size
group_of = np.repeat(np.arange(n_groups), group_size)

def fit_grouped(p_group, hidden=True, seed=0, steps=5000):
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    model = TMSHidden(n, m, k, gen) if hidden else TMS(n, m, gen)
    sampler = lambda b, g: sample_grouped(b, n_groups, group_size, p_group, g)
    train(model, sampler, None, steps=steps, seed=seed)
    return model

runs = {("sparse", True): fit_grouped(0.05, True),
        ("dense",  True): fit_grouped(0.50, True),
        ("sparse", False): fit_grouped(0.05, False),
        ("dense",  False): fit_grouped(0.50, False)}


First, what the bottleneck does with correlated inputs. The cosine matrix between the 20 input directions W_i shows whether the model gave each group a shared direction.


Cosine between input directions
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.2, 6))
for r, regime in enumerate(["sparse", "dense"]):
    for c, hidden in enumerate([False, True]):
        W = runs[(regime, hidden)].W
        C = cosine_matrix(W)
        ax = axes[r, c]
        ax.imshow(C, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
        for gb in range(group_size, n, group_size):
            ax.axhline(gb-0.5, color="k", lw=0.6); ax.axvline(gb-0.5, color="k", lw=0.6)
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
        ax.set_title(f"{regime}, {'with' if hidden else 'no'} hidden layer", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()





Cosine similarity between the bottleneck directions W_i of the 20 inputs, which come in 4 correlated groups of 5 (block boundaries drawn). Left pair: original toy with no hidden layer. Right pair: with a hidden layer. Rows: groups rarely on (sparse) and often on (dense).




Reading the figure. Without a hidden layer (left column) the toy behaves as the paper says: sparse groups are packed input by input, with no block structure, exactly as if the inputs were independent; dense groups get the “PCA-like” solution in which each group of five shares one direction. With a hidden layer (right column) the block structure appears even in the sparse regime: related inputs are written to a shared direction and the hidden neurons read that direction. That is the essay’s “related inputs grew onto the neurons”.
Second, what the hidden neurons read. For each hidden neuron j we take the cosine of its read direction V_j with each of the four group directions, defined as the mean of each group’s W_i. The sign matters: a neuron that is positive on one group and negative on another is a contrast between two things, which is what the essay calls a gate with two poles, not a mixture.


Hidden neurons in the group basis
def group_cosines(model):
    W = model.W.detach(); V = model.V.detach()
    G = torch.stack([W[:, group_of == g].mean(1) for g in range(n_groups)], 1)  # (m, n_groups)
    G = G / G.norm(dim=0, keepdim=True)
    Vn = V / V.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True).clamp_min(1e-8)
    return (Vn @ G).numpy()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
for ax, regime in zip(axes, ["sparse", "dense"]):
    cs = group_cosines(runs[(regime, True)])
    order = np.lexsort((-np.abs(cs).max(1), np.abs(cs).argmax(1)))
    im = ax.imshow(cs[order], cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(n_groups)); ax.set_xticklabels([f"g{g}" for g in range(n_groups)])
    ax.set_ylabel("hidden neuron"); ax.set_title(regime)
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="cos(V_j, group direction)")





Each row is one hidden neuron; each column a group of correlated inputs. Colour is the cosine between the neuron’s read direction V_j and that group’s shared direction. Left: sparse groups. Right: dense groups. A neuron ‘about’ one group is a single strong cell; a contrast neuron has one red and one blue cell.





The pole-by-pole audit of the hidden neurons that follows is our own analysis. The essay’s figure for this variant shows only the bottleneck’s cosine structure.

Because the output ReLU discards a neuron’s negative side, what the neuron transmits is its positive pole. So the fair question, in the essay’s own terms, is whether the positive pole is about one group. We count a neuron as “one group on the positive pole” if, among the groups it reads with positive sign, one carries more than 80% of the positive weight; we also record whether it has a strong negative pole on some other group.


Summary over several seeds
def classify(model):
    cs = group_cosines(model); V = model.V.detach()
    alive = (V.norm(dim=1) > 1e-2).numpy()
    pos = np.clip(cs, 0, None) ** 2
    share = pos.max(1) / np.maximum(pos.sum(1), 1e-8)
    return alive, share > 0.8, cs.min(1) < -0.5

print(f"{'regime':8s} {'alive':>6s} {'one-group +pole':>16s} {'…with strong -pole':>19s} {'mixed +pole':>12s}   (5 seeds x {k} neurons)")
for regime, p in [("sparse", 0.05), ("dense", 0.5)]:
    tot = np.zeros(4)
    for seed in range(5):
        alive, one, neg = classify(fit_grouped(p, True, seed=seed, steps=4000))
        tot += [alive.sum(), (one & alive).sum(), (one & neg & alive).sum(), (~one & alive).sum()]
    print(f"{regime:8s} {tot[0]:6.0f} {tot[1]:16.0f} {tot[2]:19.0f} {tot[3]:12.0f}")


regime    alive  one-group +pole  …with strong -pole  mixed +pole   (5 seeds x 10 neurons)
sparse       50               31                  10           19
dense        50               22                  12           28


The result is intermediate, and worth stating plainly rather than rounding toward either side. Roughly three in five hidden neurons in the sparse regime, and about half in the dense regime, have a positive pole that is about one group; a third of those also carry a strong negative pole on another group, which is the “V versus O” structure the essay describes. The remaining neurons read a positive combination of two groups. No neuron reads all four. Widening the hidden layer to 20 neurons does not change the proportions. (Making the groups fire more often makes the bottleneck more PCA-like, as the essay says, but it does not make the hidden neurons cleaner in this count.)
One caution on reading this. The groups here are independent of each other, so a neuron reading two groups is a mixture of unrelated things in the essay’s sense. Adding correlations and a hidden layer makes the bottleneck organise by group and gives many neurons a one-group positive pole, but it does not make mixed neurons disappear. Whether real networks are in a regime where two-group neurons are rare is exactly what the rest of the essay tries to show empirically, and it is not something a toy can settle.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
section: 6. Adding the missing benefit: readers instead of reconstruction
text:
6. Adding the missing benefit: readers instead of reconstruction
Section 5 put the relatedness into the data. But in a toy with independent inputs there is nothing intrinsically related about any two of them: every partition into groups is a relabelling of every other. So any grouping we saw there could be credited to the input statistics. The essay’s argument is about something else: a representation matters only through what reads it, and sharing a direction between two inputs is a benefit when downstream readers want them together. The original toy has no readers, so that benefit is priced at zero. Here we put readers in and leave the inputs exactly as in the original toy: independent and sparse.
The setup. The bottleneck h = Wx feeds a hidden ReLU layer, which feeds T = 12 output tasks. Every task has the same form: a rectified sum over five inputs, y_t = \mathrm{ReLU}\big(\sum_{i \in S_t} x_i - \theta_t\big), with \theta_t cycling through three thresholds. The only thing we vary is how many distinct subsets S_t the twelve tasks factor through, which we call J:

J = 4: four disjoint subsets, each read by three tasks. A four-dimensional intermediate (the four sums) serves every reader. This is maximal reuse.
J = 12: twelve subsets chosen to overlap as little as possible, each read by one task. No shared intermediate helps anyone. This is the control.
J = 6, 8 in between.

With J = 4 and only four tasks the two conditions would be identical, which is the relabelling point again; the difference appears only when several readers want the same combination. That is what the essay calls reuse, so J is the quantity under test rather than a proxy for it.
What to measure, without reference to any grouping the data does not contain: the participation ratio of the singular values of W (the effective number of bottleneck dimensions in use), the mean |cosine| between input directions for pairs that share a subset versus pairs that share none, the task loss, and the hidden-neuron poles scored against the task-defined subsets.


Train the reader toy across the reuse knob J
from common.toy_models import (ReaderToy, make_subsets, make_tasks, train_tasks,
                               participation_ratio, within_between_cosine)
n, m, k, T, fan, S_READ = 20, 5, 20, 12, 5, 0.9

def fit_readers(J, S=S_READ, seed=0, steps=4000, extra_tasks=()):
    subs = make_subsets(n, J, fan, seed=seed)
    tasks = make_tasks(subs, T) + list(extra_tasks(subs) if callable(extra_tasks) else extra_tasks)
    model = ReaderToy(n, m, k, len(tasks), torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed))
    L = train_tasks(model, tasks, n, S, steps=steps, seed=seed)
    return model, subs, tasks, L[-200:].mean()

Js = [4, 6, 8, 12]
reader_runs = {J: [fit_readers(J, seed=s) for s in range(2)] for J in Js}
print(f"{'J':>3s} {'max overlap':>12s} {'loss':>8s} {'PR':>6s} {'|cos| within':>13s} {'between':>8s}   (S = {S_READ}, 2 seeds)")
for J in Js:
    rows = []
    for model, subs, _, loss in reader_runs[J]:
        w, b = within_between_cosine(model.W, subs)
        rows.append((loss, participation_ratio(model.W), w, b))
    r = np.mean(rows, 0)
    subs = reader_runs[J][0][1]
    ov = max(len(set(a) & set(b)) for i, a in enumerate(subs) for b in subs[i+1:])
    print(f"{J:3d} {ov:12d} {r[0]:8.3f} {r[1]:6.2f} {r[2]:13.2f} {r[3]:8.2f}")


  J  max overlap     loss     PR  |cos| within  between   (S = 0.9, 2 seeds)
  4            0    0.005   4.13          0.81     0.18
  6            2    0.086   4.23          0.61     0.22
  8            2    0.173   4.51          0.51     0.24
 12            2    0.388   4.61          0.42     0.25




Input directions, ordered by subset, at the two ends of the knob
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.2, 3.6))
for ax, J in zip(axes, [4, 12]):
    model, subs, _, _ = reader_runs[J][0]
    first = {}
    for j, s in enumerate(subs):
        for i in s: first.setdefault(i, j)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (first.get(i, 99), i))
    C = cosine_matrix(model.W)[np.ix_(order, order)]
    ax.imshow(C, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    if J == 4:
        for gb in range(fan, n, fan):
            ax.axhline(gb-0.5, color="k", lw=0.6); ax.axvline(gb-0.5, color="k", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_title(f"J = {J}")
plt.tight_layout()





Cosine between the bottleneck directions W_i of the 20 independent inputs, ordered by the task subsets (boundaries drawn), for maximal reuse (J=4, left) and no reuse (J=12, right; inputs ordered by their first subset). The inputs are statistically identical in both panels; only the readers differ.




With maximal reuse the bottleneck becomes four coarse directions, one per shared sum, with the five inputs of each sum nearly parallel (|cosine| about 0.8 within, 0.2 between) and a participation ratio of 4. Nothing about the inputs asked for this; the readers did. With no reuse the same inputs are spread with no block structure, the participation ratio rises toward 5, and the task loss is seventy times larger: twelve independent sums do not fit in five dimensions, so the network packs them with interference. Intermediate J gives intermediate values of everything.
Two remarks on the control. First, it is the original toy’s situation transposed up one level: the quantities being packed are now the readers’ sums rather than the inputs, but the mechanism is the same. Second, the control is not a strawman. Each task still reads five inputs through the same function; it just reads a combination nobody else wants.


Hidden-neuron poles against the task subsets
def subset_cosines(model, subs):
    W = model.W.detach(); V = model.V.detach()
    G = torch.stack([W[:, s].mean(1) for s in subs], 1); G = G / G.norm(dim=0, keepdim=True)
    Vn = V / V.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True).clamp_min(1e-8)
    return (Vn @ G).numpy()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [4, 12]})
for ax, J in zip(axes, [4, 12]):
    model, subs, _, _ = reader_runs[J][0]
    cs = subset_cosines(model, subs)
    order = np.lexsort((-np.abs(cs).max(1), np.abs(cs).argmax(1)))
    im = ax.imshow(cs[order], cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xlabel("task subset"); ax.set_title(f"J = {J}")
axes[0].set_ylabel("hidden neuron")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="cos(V_j, subset direction)")

Does sparsity rescue the no-reuse control?
S_list = [0.0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.97]
curves = {J: [] for J in (4, 12)}
for Sp in S_list:
    for J in (4, 12):
        rows = []
        for s in range(2):
            model, subs, _, loss = fit_readers(J, S=Sp, seed=s)
            w, b = within_between_cosine(model.W, subs)
            rows.append((loss, w - b))
        curves[J].append(np.mean(rows, 0))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.2))
for J, lab in [(4, "J = 4 (reuse)"), (12, "J = 12 (no reuse)")]:
    c = np.array(curves[J])
    axes[0].plot(S_list, c[:, 0], "o-", label=lab); axes[1].plot(S_list, c[:, 1], "o-", label=lab)
axes[0].set_yscale("log"); axes[0].set_xlabel("sparsity S"); axes[0].set_ylabel("task loss"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xlabel("sparsity S"); axes[1].set_ylabel("|cos| within − between")
plt.tight_layout()





Task loss (left) and the gap between within-subset and between-subset |cosine| (right) as a function of input sparsity, for maximal reuse and no reuse. Two seeds each.




The reuse condition is clean and nearly lossless at every sparsity. The no-reuse condition is simply infeasible when inputs are dense, and only approaches a low loss at very high sparsity, where packing with interference becomes cheap. This is the original toy’s phase diagram again, now driven by the readers: superposition is what a network does when the things it must represent are unrelated to its readers and rare enough to pack.

A private offshoot
If reuse makes inputs coarse, what happens when one reader wants fine structure? We keep the J = 4 tasks and add a single extra task that reads one input alone, y = x_{i^\star} for some i^\star in the first subset. The prediction from the essay’s picture is that W_{i^\star} stays aligned with its group direction and grows a private component that the rest of the group lacks.


One extra reader on a single input
def offshoot_stats(extra, seeds=3):
    out = []
    for s in range(seeds):
        ex = (lambda subs: [([subs[0][0]], 0.0)]) if extra else ()
        model, subs, _, loss = fit_readers(4, seed=s, extra_tasks=ex)
        W = model.W.detach(); g = W[:, subs[0]].mean(1); g = g / g.norm()
        def split(i):
            w = W[:, i]; par = float(w @ g); return par, float((w - par * g).norm())
        t = split(subs[0][0]); o = np.mean([split(i) for i in subs[0][1:]], 0)
        out.append((loss, t[0], t[1], o[0], o[1]))
    return np.mean(out, 0)
print(f"{'extra reader':>13s} {'loss':>7s} {'target ∥ group':>15s} {'target ⊥':>9s} {'others ∥ group':>15s} {'others ⊥':>9s}")
for extra in (False, True):
    r = offshoot_stats(extra)
    print(f"{str(extra):>13s} {r[0]:7.3f} {r[1]:15.2f} {r[2]:9.2f} {r[3]:15.2f} {r[4]:9.2f}")


 extra reader    loss  target ∥ group  target ⊥  others ∥ group  others ⊥
        False   0.005            0.90      0.18            0.92      0.35
         True   0.015            0.92      1.21            0.91      0.39


The single extra reader makes the target input’s private component more than six times larger while leaving its alignment with the group untouched, and leaves the other four members of the group as they were. In the essay’s language, the input has a group direction and an offshoot, and the offshoot exists because something reads it. This is the smallest possible model of “recursive generalisation”: a coarse representation that grows a finer branch exactly where a downstream reader needs one.


What this adds to the picture

The relatedness that makes a network group things is not in the inputs. It is in the readers. Identical input statistics give clean coarse directions under shared readers and packing under unshared ones.
Superposition and generalisation are not two learning principles here; they are what one objective does in two regimes of reader structure. Packing wins only when the quantities readers need are unrelated to each other and sparse enough to overlap cheaply.
What the toy cannot tell us is which regime a real network’s readers are in. The essay’s bet is that in real data “almost nothing is related to nothing”, so real readers are overwhelmingly of the shared kind. That is the empirical claim the rest of the essay has to carry.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
section: 7. What to carry into the essay
text:
7. What to carry into the essay

Packing is real and robust in the toy’s world. Independent sparse features in a narrow bottleneck with nothing downstream get packed into polytopes, with discrete phase changes.
Correlation plus a hidden layer changes the picture, partly. Related inputs share directions in the bottleneck, and about half to two thirds of hidden neurons have a one-group positive pole, some with a contrasting negative pole. This is the mechanism the essay calls generalisation, and it appears as soon as the toy has somewhere for related things to grow. But a sizeable minority of neurons still read two unrelated groups, so the toy supports the essay’s mechanism without supporting its strong claim.
The toy cannot say which regime real networks are in. That is an empirical question and it is what the essay’s vision and language experiments are for.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
section: 8. What the toy does and does not say
text:
8. What the toy does and does not say
The toy’s results are robust and the essay accepts them: when independent, sparse features must be squeezed through a narrow linear bottleneck and reconstructed, the optimum packs them into non-orthogonal polytopes, with discrete phase changes as sparsity varies.
The essay’s objection is to three modelling choices that it argues do not hold in real networks:

Features are given in advance and independent. In a real network nothing is defined in advance; everything is grown, and real data has structure at every scale (“a rare person still has a country, a job and a name”).
Nothing reads the representation. The loss is reconstruction, so each feature is an end in itself. In a real network a representation only matters through what downstream reads it, and sharing a direction between related things is a benefit (reuse), not a cost.
There are no hidden neurons in the main experiments. Superposition in the toy is about directions in a bottleneck; reports of polysemanticity in real networks are about mixtures in neurons. The paper itself studies hidden neurons and correlated features, but separately.

The toy therefore predicts where to expect packing: memories that are ends in themselves and related to nothing else. The essay’s claim is that real networks are rarely in that regime, and the rest of the essay is an attempt to show this empirically in vision and language models.

title: Background: Toy Models of Superposition
text:
Questions from the reading group
Raised in discussion on 22 October 2026. The answers are ours, not the essay’s.
What does the readers experiment in section 6 actually test? If the number of independent tasks exceeds the bottleneck, isn’t the network simply forced into something like superposition?
At the endpoints, yes, the outcome is forced by counting. Twelve independent sums cannot pass losslessly through five dimensions, so the network must drop some or pack them with interference; four sums can, so it does. The toy discovers nothing there.
What it tests is a claim that is often read into the original toy: that more features than dimensions implies superposition. In both of our conditions there are twenty inputs and five dimensions, and in both the inputs are independent and sparse, so the original toy’s premise holds identically. Yet with shared readers the network does not pack the twenty inputs at all. It builds four coarse directions and discards the within-group identity that nobody downstream asked for. The relevant count is not “features versus dimensions” but “what the readers need versus dimensions”, and when readers want shared things the answer is coarse-and-clean rather than packed. That is the essay’s “coarser, never fractured” in its smallest form.
The non-trivial content is at the margins rather than the endpoints. With six or eight distinct sums the required information exceeds the bottleneck but overlaps partially, and the network’s compromise is intermediate rather than a switch. When packing is forced, it only becomes cheap at high sparsity, so the original phase boundary reappears for the readers’ quantities, which supports reading superposition as what one objective does in one regime rather than as a second principle. And the offshoot test shows that a single reader is enough to grow a private direction inside a coarse one.
A tighter version would hold the dimension of what readers need fixed and vary only its structure: for instance eight tasks on subsets that overlap hierarchically against eight on subsets that overlap at random. That would separate “how much information” from “how organised the information is”, which is closer to the essay’s real claim. Not yet built.

title: Cars and Animals
text:
The essay’s first piece of evidence is a reinterpretation of the most famous polysemantic neuron in the field, InceptionV1’s 4e:55 (channel 55 of layer mixed4e). Zoom In (2020) presented it as responding to cat faces and car fronts and said outright that it “isn’t responding to some commonality of cars and cat faces”. The essay now says it is a V-shape neuron: pointed things drive it positive, round things drive it negative, and the cats and cars are two of many things with a V in them.
The original 2014 InceptionV1 weights are public (the inception5h graph that the Lucid and Lucent libraries ship), so this is a claim we can check directly. We do not have ImageNet, so we use the 5,000 COCO validation images instead, which have cats, cars, dogs and much else, and which come with object labels we can use for statistics.

title: Cars and Animals
text:
What the essay claims, specifically

The neuron’s strongest inputs from the previous layer include 4d:493 (fox snout), 4d:477 (wolf face) and 4d:201 (van front); its strongest reader downstream is 5a:94 (V-shaped flames).
Its negative pole is “an O, round where the V is pointed”.
Its positive pole generalises beyond cats and cars to anything pointed: fox faces, pool tables, bullet trains.
Therefore the right description is a shared pattern (a verb, “pointed versus round”), not a list of nouns (cats OR cars).

Claims 1 and 2 are checkable from the weights and from any photo collection. Claim 3 we can check partially with COCO’s labels. Claim 4 is an interpretation, and the last section discusses how much the evidence supports it.


Setup: load the original InceptionV1 and scan COCO (cached after the first run)
import sys, pathlib, json, numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image
ROOT = pathlib.Path.cwd().parent

from common.inception import load_inceptionv1, scan_layer, receptive_crop

CH = 55
model = load_inceptionv1(DEV)
paths = sorted((ROOT / "data/coco/val2017").glob("*.jpg"))
cache = ROOT / "data/cache/mixed4e_1x1_prerelu_coco.npz"
if cache.exists():
    z = dict(np.load(cache))
else:
    res = scan_layer(model, "mixed4e_1x1_pre_relu_conv", paths, device=DEV, batch=100)
    np.savez_compressed(cache, **{k: v for k, v in res.items() if k != "paths"}, paths=np.array(res["paths"]))
    z = dict(np.load(cache))
mx, mn, grid = z["max"][:, CH], z["min"][:, CH], int(z["grid"][0])
print(f"{len(paths)} images; 4e:55 pre-ReLU spatial max: median {np.median(mx):.0f}, "
      f"99th pct {np.percentile(mx, 99):.0f}, top {mx.max():.0f}; spatial min: bottom {mn.min():.0f}")


5000 images; 4e:55 pre-ReLU spatial max: median 196, 99th pct 766, top 1719; spatial min: bottom -575


A note on what is measured. mixed4e is a concatenation of four branches and channel 55 is in the 1×1 branch, so we hook that branch’s convolution before its ReLU. That way the negative pole is visible; after the ReLU it would be zero everywhere. For each image we record the maximum and minimum over the 14×14 spatial grid and where they occur, and show a crop around that location as a stand-in for the receptive field.

The two poles on 5,000 photographs

pos = sheet(np.argsort(-mx), z["argmax_yx"]); neg = sheet(np.argsort(mn), z["argmin_yx"])

Left: crops around the location of the 40 strongest positive responses of 4e:55 in COCO val2017. Right: the 40 strongest negative responses. Each crop is about 45% of the 224-pixel input, centred on the activation’s location.




The positive sheet is the famous grid: frontal cat faces and the fronts of cars, with a couple of small dogs. The negative sheet is clocks, the round heads of bears and cows, teddy bears, the backs of human heads, plates and bowls. The essay’s description of the negative pole as “an O” holds up on a dataset the neuron was never ranked on before.

Is it really just cats and cars? Using the labels
COCO’s instance annotations tell us what is in each image. If the neuron were an OR of cat and car, images with neither should not reach the top. If it is a V-shape detector, some should, and they should be pointed things.


Label statistics of the top images

What drives the neuron when cats and cars are excluded: frontal animal faces (goat, bighorn sheep, horse, zebra, bear, small birds), the noses of trains and aircraft, computer mice and remote controls seen end-on, and scenes with strong converging perspective lines such as tennis courts, baseball diamonds, railway tracks and bed corners. The essay’s own examples of what the V generalises to were fox faces, pool tables and bullet trains. The COCO list is the same kind of thing: pointed fronts and converging lines. This is the strongest evidence on this page for the “V, not OR(cat, car)” reading.

The circuit: inputs and readers from the weights
The essay names specific neighbours. Because mixed4e’s 1×1 branch is a 1×1 convolution, its weight matrix is directly the vector of votes each mixed4d channel casts for 4e:55, and the mixed5a convolutions give the votes 4e:55 casts for each mixed5a channel.


Rank the essay’s named inputs and reader by weight
w_in = model.mixed4e_1x1_pre_relu_conv.weight[CH, :, 0, 0].detach().cpu()
top = torch.argsort(-w_in)[:8]
print("strongest inputs from mixed4d  (channel, weight):", [(int(i), round(float(w_in[i]), 3)) for i in top])
for c, name in [(493, "fox snout"), (477, "wolf face"), (201, "van front")]:
    print(f"  essay's 4d:{c} ({name}): weight {float(w_in[c]):+.3f}, rank {int((w_in > w_in[c]).sum())+1} of 528")
w1 = model.mixed5a_1x1_pre_relu_conv.weight[:, CH, 0, 0].detach().cpu()
print("strongest readers in mixed5a 1x1 branch:", [(int(i), round(float(w1[i]), 3)) for i in torch.argsort(-w1)[:6]])
print(f"  essay's 5a:94 (V-shaped flames): weight {float(w1[94]):+.3f}, rank {int((w1 > w1[94]).sum())+1} of 256")


strongest inputs from mixed4d  (channel, weight): [(493, 0.311), (511, 0.128), (61, 0.116), (352, 0.102), (334, 0.08), (383, 0.079), (143, 0.072), (477, 0.068)]

  essay's 4d:477 (wolf face): weight +0.068, rank 8 of 528
  essay's 4d:201 (van front): weight +0.057, rank 15 of 528
strongest readers in mixed5a 1x1 branch: [(94, 0.1), (240, 0.058), (81, 0.057), (254, 0.057), (102, 0.057), (62, 0.055)]

The essay’s named input 4d:493 is the single strongest weight into the neuron, by a factor of more than two over the next, and its named reader 5a:94 is the single strongest reader in that branch. The other two named inputs are in the top fifteen of 528. These are raw weights rather than data-weighted attributions, so the agreement is if anything stronger than the essay needed. (We have not visualised 4d:493 or 5a:94 ourselves; the labels “fox snout” and “V-shaped flames” are the essay’s.)

title: Cars and Animals
section: A synthetic probe: does a bare V excite it?

title: Cars and Animals
text:
Assessment

Confirmed on public weights: the named inputs and reader are the strongest by weight; the negative pole is round things; the positive pole extends beyond cats and cars to frontal animal faces, vehicle noses and converging lines.
Supported but not proven: that “pointed versus round” is the right one-line description. It fits everything we saw, and it fits better than OR(cat, car), which cannot explain the goats, trains and tennis courts. A line-drawn V alone is not enough, so the description is of a high-level shape cue, not a contour.
Not addressed here: the second half of the essay’s section, the car-into-dogs circuit and the “generalised pose neurons”. That needs feature visualisation with and without the bias toward natural paths, which is the subject of the next section.

title: Cars and Animals
text:
Questions from the reading group
Raised in discussion on 22 October 2026. The answers are ours, not the essay’s.
Before the essay, was the idea that 4e:55 fired on both cats and cars because it was helping encode those two features in superposition, with many other neurons firing too?
Roughly yes, with a historical wrinkle. Zoom In (2020) described 4e:55 as responding to cat faces, cat legs and car fronts, and offered superposition as a hypothesis for why: a network that needs more features than it has neurons folds several into one, and a neuron that is “OR(cat, car)” is the visible symptom. Toy Models of Superposition only made this precise in 2022. Under the precise version a feature is a direction in activation space, and if the car direction is not neuron-aligned it spans several neurons: 4e:55 carries a piece of “car” and a piece of “cat”, other neurons carry other pieces, and a downstream reader recovers “car” by the linear combination that cancels the cat part. Interference is tolerable because cats and cars rarely co-occur. The car-into-dogs circuit was read the same way, as the car being stored across several dog neurons for later decoding.
The essay’s rebuttal is aimed at the decoding step. If that were the mechanism, some downstream weight pattern would have to read the cancelling combination. The essay says none does: the readers of 4e:55 use it as one thing (its strongest reader is a V-shaped-flame neuron, which we confirmed from the weights above), and the dog neurons the car writes into are shared pose neurons feeding car specialists. “Nothing reads that combination” turns a question about appearances into a question about weights.
The neuron does not fire strongly for a literal drawn V. How should we make sense of the “V-shape” label? Is it “V-shapes in objects”?
Yes, and we would go a little further. A neuron at mixed4e is defined by its inputs, and its strongest inputs are already part detectors: a fox snout, a wolf face, a van front. What those share is a pointed, convergent frontal structure built from the textures and parts that mid-level neurons respond to. A line drawing has the geometry but none of the parts, so it drives none of the inputs and therefore barely drives the neuron. The essay’s own footnote says this: to see the shared pattern you have to visualise what the neuron’s inputs have in common, not the neuron on its own.
So “V” is a compression of “pointed convergent front, as it appears in natural objects”. The COCO result supports that compression, since goats, horses, train noses, aircraft and converging court lines all drive it, which OR(cat, car) cannot explain. What the evidence does not settle is whether “V” is a better label than “frontal pointed object”. A sharper synthetic test would use photographic crops of pointed things with no face, such as boat bows, roof gables and arrowheads, rather than drawn lines.

title: Cars and Animals
text:
Discussion questions

The neuron fires on cat faces far more strongly than on anything else in COCO. Is a neuron whose top of the distribution is 85% cats, but whose tail is “pointed things”, best called a cat neuron, a V neuron, or something else? Does the answer depend on what reads it?
The essay’s recommended trick is to describe a neuron without nouns. Try it on the negative-pole sheet above. Is “round” the only candidate?
How would one tell a “V-shape” neuron from a “frontal face or front of object” neuron? What stimulus would separate them?
